mcq.q: Only 2% of tickets are urgent. A model predicting "not urgent" for everything scores…
options: 2% accuracy, the share of urgent tickets
50% accuracy, no better than a coin flip
98% accuracy but 0% urgent recall
98% recall on urgent and 2% precision
mcq.why: Accuracy rewards the majority class; recall on the rare class reveals the failure.
distractors: Predicting the majority class for every ticket is right 98% of the time, not 2%.
50% would need half the predictions wrong; the majority class alone gives 98%.
Recall on urgent tickets is 0%: the model never predicts urgent.

mcq.q: How is agreement between two annotators commonly measured?
options: Accuracy of the model
Mean squared error
Cohen's κ (kappa)
Perplexity
mcq.why: κ corrects raw agreement for agreement expected by chance. Low agreement means the task is ambiguous, which caps any model.
distractors: Model accuracy is a different question.
MSE measures regression error.
Perplexity measures language models.

mcq.q: Two annotators label 200 tickets and reach κ = 0.58 on “urgent”. What is the right next step?
options: Label 10,000 more tickets now and let the volume average out disagreement
Revise the guideline for the disputed cases before labelling more
Train the model now and treat the disagreement as ordinary noise
Drop the urgent class and keep only labels the annotators agree on
mcq.why: Disagreement shows the definition is unclear; fix it first or the labels will be noisy.
distractors: More labels under an unclear guideline multiply the same disagreement.
κ = 0.58 means the label itself is unclear; the model will learn the confusion.
Urgent is the class the business needs; fix the definition instead.

mcq.q: Which are remedies for class imbalance? Choose all that apply.
options: Resampling
Class weights
Tuning the decision threshold
Reporting accuracy only
mcq.why: Weights, resampling and threshold tuning all help, measured with precision and recall.
distractors: Accuracy hides the rare class: predicting the majority scores high.

mcq.q: You oversample the rare class and then split into train and test. What goes wrong?
options: Copies of the same example land in both train and test, inflating scores
The rare class disappears from the training data entirely
Nothing, as long as the copies are exact duplicates
Training becomes impossible because the classes are now equal
mcq.why: Split first, then resample only the training split.
distractors: Oversampling adds copies of the rare class; it does not remove it.
Exact copies in both sets are the problem: the model is tested on what it trained on.
Balanced classes train fine; the evaluation is what breaks.

mcq.q: Features must be computed using only information available…
options: From the test set
At any time, including the future
After the outcome is known
At prediction time
mcq.why: Anything known only later leaks the answer and fails in production.
distractors: Test data must stay unseen.
Future information is leakage.
That is exactly the leakage trap.

mcq.q: Why add an is_missing flag instead of only filling missing values?
options: Models cannot read numbers
Missingness itself is often informative
Flags make the data smaller
It removes the need for cleaning
mcq.why: Whether a value is missing can correlate with the outcome, so keep that signal.
distractors: Models read numbers fine.
A flag adds a column.
Cleaning is still needed.

mcq.q: With 2% positives, what class weight on positives (negatives ÷ positives) balances the classes?
distractors: That would be 100 ÷ 2.
That is the positive fraction.
That is the positive percentage.

mcq.q: Near-duplicate documents end up split across train and test. What happens to your scores?
options: Nothing, because near-duplicates are not exact copies
Training fails because the same text appears twice
They look better than they will be in production
They look worse than production, because duplicates confuse the model
mcq.why: The model has effectively seen test examples, which is leakage (3.4).
distractors: Near-duplicates let the model recognise test items it has nearly seen.
Training runs fine; only the evaluation is distorted.
Leakage across splits makes scores look better, not worse.

mcq.q: Why keep raw data immutable?
options: So you can rebuild the training table when code or raw data changes
Because editing large raw files in place is slow
So the labels can never change once they are written
To save disk space by never storing a second copy
mcq.why: Each preparation step is versioned code over untouched raw data.
distractors: Speed is not the reason; reproducibility is.
Labels can be revised; they are versioned separately from raw data.
Immutable raw data plus derived tables usually uses more space.

interview.q: Why does data quality often matter more than model choice?
covers: Models learn whatever is in the data
Most project time is spent here
interview.followUp: Give an example where fixing the data helped more than changing the model.

interview.q: How do you handle class imbalance?
covers: Use precision, recall and PR curves
interview.followUp: Your model's precision at the chosen threshold is too low. What do you try?

interview.q: What makes a good labelling guideline?
interview.followUp: κ is 0.45 after the pilot. What do you do next?

interview.q: Your annotators agree only 60% of the time. What do you do?
covers: Find which cases they disagree on
interview.followUp: When would you accept a low agreement ceiling?

interview.q: Walk through engineering features for a fraud model.
covers: Counts and sums over recent windows
Deviation from the customer's own history
Everything computed as of the prediction time
interview.followUp: How do you make sure these features are computed the same way in training and in production?

interview.q: Cancellation labels at {company} are only final after the travel date. How do you build the training set?
covers: Include only bookings whose travel date has passed
Compute features as of booking time
Exclude post-event columns such as fees
interview.followUp: Waiting for the travel date makes the labels months old. How do you keep the model current?

interview.q: Design a labelling pipeline for 10,000 support tickets.
covers: Pilot with double labelling and κ
interview.followUp: How would you use an LLM to speed this up without lowering label quality?

interview.q: Design {company}'s fraud training-data pipeline so it never leaks the label.
covers: No post-event columns such as chargeback flags
interview.followUp: Chargebacks arrive up to 90 days late. How does that change your validation split?

mcq.q: Which is leakage when predicting churn on day 3?
options: Using the plan type the customer chose
Using total refunds this month
Splitting the data by customer ID
Using a validation set to pick settings
mcq.why: Month-total refunds include future information that is not available on day 3.
distractors: Plan type is known on day 3, so it is a legitimate feature.
Splitting by customer is how you prevent leakage, not a leak.
A validation set is part of a sound protocol.

mcq.q: What is the validation set for?
options: Fitting the model's weights to the examples
Choosing settings and comparing variants
A final, one-time estimate of performance
Storing raw data that is never changed
mcq.why: The test set is held back and used once at the end.
distractors: Weights are fitted on the training set.
That is the test set's job.
Raw-data storage is unrelated to splits.

mcq.q: What is overfitting?
options: A model too simple to capture the real pattern in the data
Memorising training noise, so training error is low but new-data error is high
Training on more data than the model can usefully learn from
Stopping training after too few steps for the model to settle
mcq.why: Generalisation, performing well on new data, is what matters.
distractors: That is underfitting.
More data usually reduces overfitting.
Stopping early is a remedy for overfitting, not its cause.

mcq.q: Which of these is not a regularisation technique?
options: An L2 (ridge) penalty on the model's weights
Early stopping when validation loss rises
Adding more features computed from the label
Limiting tree depth and the number of leaves
mcq.why: Features computed from the label are leakage, not regularisation.
distractors: An L2 penalty shrinks weights and is a classic regulariser.
Early stopping limits training before the model fits noise.
Limiting depth constrains model complexity.

mcq.q: A churn model used days since last login, computed at extraction time. Offline AUC was 0.97; in production it was 0.68. What is the fix?
options: Lower the decision threshold to catch more churners
Compute features as of the prediction date (a point-in-time join)
Use a bigger model that can learn the harder production data
Retrain more often so the model keeps up with production
mcq.why: For churned customers the feature was large only because they had already left: future information leaked in.
distractors: The model's inputs were wrong offline; a threshold cannot fix leakage.
The gap comes from leaked features, not model capacity.
Retraining on leaked features repeats the same mistake.

mcq.q: How should you split time-dependent data?
options: Put the newest data in training and older data in test
Split randomly so both sets cover every period
Split alphabetically by customer name to keep it simple
Train on the past, test on the future
mcq.why: A random split leaks the future into training.
distractors: That trains on the future and tests on the past.
A random split leaks future patterns into training.
Alphabetical order is arbitrary and ignores time.

mcq.q: The same customer appears in both train and test. What split prevents this?
options: A random split with a fixed seed
Shuffling the rows twice before splitting
A larger test set that dilutes the overlap
A group split by customer
mcq.why: Grouping keeps all of one customer's rows on the same side, so the model cannot memorise their habits.
distractors: A random split puts the same customer's rows in both sets.
Shuffling more does not keep customers together.
The overlap remains and still inflates scores.

mcq.q: You check the test set after every change and adjust the model. What happens?
options: Nothing, as long as each adjustment you make is small
The test set gets more reliable with every check that you run on it
The model generalises better because it is tested more often
The test set turns into validation data, so its estimate stops being trustworthy
mcq.why: Use the test set once; tune on validation.
distractors: Many small choices tuned to the test set add up to overfitting it.
Every check fits the model more closely to it, so it gets less reliable.
It fits this test set better, not new data.

mcq.q: What is benchmark contamination for LLMs?
options: Benchmark questions appeared in the pretraining data
A tokenizer bug that splits benchmark questions differently
Running the same benchmark twice and averaging the results
Benchmarks whose questions are too hard for current models
mcq.why: If the model saw the questions, its score overstates real ability (8.6).
distractors: That is a tokenisation issue, not contamination.
Repeating a run is ordinary practice.
Difficulty is not contamination.

mcq.q: In the overfitting figure, at a high polynomial degree you raise λ (the ridge penalty). What happens?
options: Validation error rises further as the curve bends more
The curve smooths and validation error recovers
Training error falls further as the penalty grows
Nothing changes, because the degree fixes the curve
mcq.why: Penalising large weights reduces the wiggles that fit noise.
distractors: A larger penalty reduces wiggles, which lowers validation error here.
The penalty trades training fit for smoothness, so training error rises.
The penalty changes the fitted weights at any degree.

interview.q: Explain train, validation and test sets, and why each exists.
covers: Test once for a final estimate
Why reusing the test set breaks it
interview.followUp: You have only 2,000 labelled examples. How do you split them?

interview.q: What is overfitting, and how do you detect it?
covers: Training error low, new-data error high
interview.followUp: Training more data did not close the gap. What next?

interview.q: What is data leakage? Give three examples.
covers: Same user in train and test
interview.followUp: Which of your examples would an automated check catch, and which would it miss?

interview.q: Offline AUC is 0.97, production 0.68. How do you investigate?
covers: Check each feature's availability at prediction time
Compare offline and online feature values
interview.followUp: Which single check would you do first, and why?

interview.q: How would you split data for a model that predicts customer churn?
covers: Features as of the prediction date
interview.followUp: How long a gap would you leave between training and test, and why?

interview.q: {company}'s return model looks perfect offline. What do you check first?
covers: Columns filled after delivery, such as refund amounts
A random split mixing sale and non-sale periods
interview.followUp: The time split drops the score from 0.98 to 0.71. What do you tell the team?

interview.q: Design an evaluation protocol that prevents leakage for a time-dependent problem.
interview.followUp: How would you detect a suspicious feature automatically?

interview.q: How do you prevent test-set overuse in a team that iterates quickly?
covers: Restrict access to the final test set
Use validation and cross-validation for iteration
interview.followUp: How would you know the test set has already been overused?

mcq.q: When is a PR curve more informative than ROC?
options: When classes are balanced
When positives are rare
Only for regression
Never
mcq.why: With rare positives, ROC can look good while precision is poor; PR curves expose that.
distractors: With balanced classes ROC is informative and PR adds little.
Both curves are for classifiers, not regression.
With rare positives, ROC can look good while precision is poor.

mcq.q: A classifier has 40 true positives, 10 false positives and 20 false negatives. What is its precision?
mcq.why: Precision = TP/(TP + FP) = 40/50 = 80%.
distractors: That mixes the counts.
That is FN/(TP + FN).
That is the recall.

mcq.q: With the same counts (TP 40, FP 10, FN 20), what is recall?
mcq.why: Recall = TP/(TP + FN) = 40/60 ≈ 67%.
distractors: 80% is precision: 40 / (40 + 10).
50% does not follow from these counts.
20 is the number of false negatives, not a rate.

mcq.q: A model has precision 0.9 and recall 0.3. What is its F1?
mcq.why: F1 = 2PR/(P + R) = 2(0.9)(0.3)/1.2 = 0.45. The harmonic mean is pulled towards the weaker of the two, so F1 is high only if both are high.
distractors: That is the precision alone.
That is the plain average; F1 is the harmonic mean.
That is the product P × R.

mcq.q: A ROC AUC of 0.5 means…
options: The decision threshold is set at 0.5
The model ranks every case perfectly
Half of the predictions are correct
The model ranks no better than random
mcq.why: AUC 0.5 is random ranking; 1.0 is perfect.
distractors: AUC summarises all thresholds; it does not set one.
A perfect ranking gives AUC 1.0.
AUC is about ranking, not the share of correct predictions.

mcq.q: What does it mean for a model to be calibrated?
options: Its accuracy on the test set is above 80%
Among cases scored 0.8, about 80% are positive
It always outputs exactly 0 or exactly 1
Its decision threshold is fixed at 0.5
mcq.why: Calibration is checked with a reliability diagram and summarised by expected calibration error.
distractors: Accuracy says nothing about whether scores match frequencies.
Hard outputs carry no probability to calibrate.
The threshold is a separate choice from calibration.

mcq.q: A missed fraud costs $400 and a false alarm costs $5 of analyst time. Where will the cost-minimising threshold sit?
options: Exactly 0.5
Low, favouring high recall
High, favouring high precision
It cannot be chosen from costs
mcq.why: Misses are 80 times more expensive than false alarms, so catching more fraud is worth more alerts.
distractors: 0.5 ignores the costs.
That would minimise false alarms, the cheap error.
Sweeping thresholds against expected cost is exactly how to choose it.

mcq.q: If a false alarm instead blocks a customer's card, costing about $60 in churn, what happens to the best threshold?
options: It moves down
It becomes 1.0
It stays the same
It moves up
mcq.why: False alarms are now more expensive, so the optimum trades some recall for precision.
distractors: Higher false-alarm cost pushes it up, not down.
1.0 would flag nothing.
The cost change moves it.

mcq.q: Platt scaling or isotonic regression for calibration should be fitted on…
options: Validation data
The training data
Production traffic without labels
The test set
mcq.why: Fitting on training data reuses the same overconfident predictions; the test set must stay untouched.
distractors: Training scores are optimistic.
Calibration needs labels.
The test set is for the final estimate.

mcq.q: An escalation classifier must keep precision at or above 80% because reviewers have limited time. How should the threshold be chosen?
options: Maximise recall subject to precision ≥ 80%
Maximise accuracy over all tickets
Maximise F1 across all thresholds
Use the default threshold of 0.5
mcq.why: The product requirement is a precision floor; F1 can pick a threshold that breaks it.
distractors: With few escalations, accuracy rewards flagging almost nothing.
F1 ignores the hard precision limit set by reviewer time.
0.5 has no link to the 80% precision requirement.

interview.q: Explain precision, recall and F1, and when each matters.
covers: Precision: how many flagged are right
Recall: how many true cases are caught
Choose by the cost of each error
interview.followUp: Which would you optimise for a fraud alert queue, and why?

interview.q: When is a PR curve more useful than a ROC curve?
covers: ROC can look good while precision is poor
PR shows the alerts a team will actually see
interview.followUp: Show me how the same model can have an excellent ROC curve and a poor PR curve.

interview.q: What does calibration mean, and how do you check it?
covers: Platt or isotonic on validation data
interview.followUp: The model is well calibrated overall but not for one segment. What do you do?

interview.q: Choose a threshold for a fraud model given the cost of a miss and of a false alarm.
interview.followUp: What changes if analysts can only review 500 alerts a day?

interview.q: Your model's AUC is 0.95, but users complain about false alarms. Explain.
covers: At a low base rate, precision can still be poor
Look at precision at the chosen threshold
Adjust the threshold or improve the model on the rare class
interview.followUp: What would you change first: the threshold or the model?

interview.q: {company} holds refunds for manual review when abuse risk is high. How do you set the threshold?
covers: Cost of delaying an honest refund versus a lost item
Monitor precision and complaints after launch
interview.followUp: The review team's capacity halves during the festival sale. What changes?

interview.q: Design a metrics dashboard for a classifier in production.
covers: Precision and recall at the operating threshold
interview.followUp: Labels arrive three weeks late. What do you show on the dashboard until then?

interview.q: How would you decide whether an LLM's self-reported confidence can trigger automatic actions?
covers: A labelled set of right and wrong outputs
Reliability diagram for the stated confidence
interview.followUp: The confidence is well calibrated today. How do you keep it that way?

mcq.q: Supervised learning learns from…
options: Rewards given for actions
Inputs that have no labels
Inputs paired with known labels
Hand-written rules
mcq.why: Examples: email → spam or not spam, house features → price.
distractors: That is reinforcement learning.
That is unsupervised learning.
Hand-written rules involve no learning at all.

mcq.q: Self-supervised learning gets its labels from…
options: Human annotators, who label every example by hand
A separate rule engine that tags the text with categories
A reward signal returned by an environment after each action
The data itself, such as the next word hidden and predicted
mcq.why: Because the labels come free from the text, pretraining can use trillions of tokens.
distractors: Self-supervised labels need no annotators.
The labels come from the data, not from rules.
That is reinforcement learning.

mcq.q: Why can LLM pretraining use trillions of tokens without human labelling?
options: Humans label every token during collection
It uses only reinforcement learning on rewards
It is self-supervised: the next token is the label
It needs no data, only a very large model
mcq.why: Every position in the text provides its own target, so no annotation is needed.
distractors: No one labels tokens; the next token is the label.
Pretraining predicts tokens; RL comes later, if at all.
Pretraining needs huge amounts of text.

mcq.q: In reinforcement learning, what does the agent learn?
options: A policy that maximises total reward from its actions
A tokenizer that splits its observations into units
A label for each example from a fixed dataset
Clusters that group similar inputs together
mcq.why: The agent acts, receives rewards and adjusts its policy to collect more reward.
distractors: Tokenizers are built separately; RL learns behaviour.
Fixed labels are supervised learning.
Clustering is unsupervised learning.

mcq.q: You want to discover customer segments with no labels at all. Which paradigm fits?
options: Supervised learning on the customer table
Reinforcement learning with a reward per segment
Hand-written rules that define each segment
Unsupervised learning, such as clustering
mcq.why: With no answers to learn from, you look for structure in the inputs.
distractors: There are no labels to supervise with.
There are no actions or rewards here.
Rules impose segments you already know; you want to discover them.

mcq.q: A shop chooses which homepage layout to show and is rewarded by clicks. Which paradigm is this?
options: A bandit, a simple form of reinforcement learning
Supervised learning on labelled layouts
Self-supervised pretraining on page text
Unsupervised learning of visitor groups
mcq.why: The system takes an action (a layout), observes a reward (clicks) and shifts towards better actions.
distractors: No one supplies the correct layout; clicks reward choices.
Nothing is predicted from hidden parts of data.
The shop takes actions and gets rewards, which is RL.

mcq.q: Predicting whether an order will be returned, from past orders with known outcomes, is…
options: Not machine learning
Reinforcement learning
Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
mcq.why: Past orders with returned or not-returned outcomes are labelled examples.
distractors: It is a standard ML problem.
Nothing is acting to collect rewards.
The outcomes are known labels.

mcq.q: A multi-step LLM agent tries tools until a task is done. Is that reinforcement learning?
options: Yes, because the agent calls tools and acts on the results
Yes, because any loop that gets feedback counts as RL
Only if it runs on GPUs while it acts, which makes it training
No, unless its weights are actually updated from a reward signal
mcq.why: Trying options at inference time is a control loop. RL means learning from reward by changing weights.
distractors: Tool use is an application design; nothing is learned.
A loop at inference time changes no weights.
Hardware has nothing to do with the learning paradigm.

mcq.q: What is the main difference between the learning paradigms?
options: The programming language and framework used to train
The size of the model and the number of its parameters
Whether a GPU or a CPU is used for the training run
The feedback: correct answers, none, or a score for actions
mcq.why: The paradigm is defined by what the learner is told, not by the model type.
distractors: Every paradigm runs in the same languages.
Any paradigm can train small or large models.
Hardware does not define the paradigm.

mcq.q: Detecting unusual transactions with no fraud labels yet is an example of…
options: Reinforcement learning
Supervised classification
Unsupervised anomaly detection
Self-supervised pretraining
mcq.why: Without labels, you flag inputs that differ from the bulk of the data.
distractors: Nothing collects reward.
There are no labels yet.
This is not predicting hidden parts of text.

interview.q: Explain supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised and reinforcement learning, with one example each.
interview.followUp: Which paradigms are used to build a chat assistant like the one you use, and in what order?

interview.q: Why is LLM pretraining called self-supervised?
covers: The next token is the label
Later stages add supervised and RL tuning
interview.followUp: What does supervised fine-tuning add after self-supervised pretraining?

interview.q: What is the feedback signal in each paradigm, and why does it matter for data collection?
covers: The signal decides what you can learn
interview.followUp: Your reward is “ticket closed”. How could a system game it?

interview.q: You have no labels for a new support category. What can you do?
covers: Weak labels from rules or an LLM
interview.followUp: How would you check that the weak labels are good enough to train on?

interview.q: When is a bandit the right tool, and what are its risks?
covers: Choosing among options with fast feedback
Guardrails for fairness and loss limits
interview.followUp: How would you stop the bandit from showing a losing option to too many users?

interview.q: Fraud labels at {company} arrive weeks after the payment. How would you combine supervised and unsupervised methods?
covers: Unsupervised anomaly signals for new patterns
interview.followUp: How would you evaluate the anomaly signals when there are no labels yet?

interview.q: Design a system that discovers new complaint themes each week and routes them.
covers: Human review names and merges clusters
Promote stable themes to supervised classes
Close the loop with routing rules
interview.followUp: How do you decide when a cluster becomes a real class?

interview.q: A team proposes RL to tune an assistant against live customer conversations. What would you require first?
covers: A reward that cannot be gamed easily
Offline evaluation before any live exposure
Clear limits on what it may change
interview.followUp: What would you measure offline before allowing any live exposure?

mcq.q: Regression predicts…
options: A category from a fixed set of classes
A group of similar points with no labels
A number, such as a price or delivery time
A reward for each action the agent takes
mcq.why: Linear regression fits y = w·x + b by minimising squared error.
distractors: That is classification.
That is clustering.
Rewards belong to reinforcement learning.

mcq.q: How does logistic regression produce a decision?
options: It clusters the points and gives each cluster a label
It splits the features into regions with a decision tree
It outputs a sigmoid probability; a threshold turns it into a decision
It outputs a category directly, with no probability involved
mcq.why: σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^−z) gives a probability; the threshold is a separate choice (3.5).
distractors: Clustering is unsupervised; logistic regression is supervised.
Trees are a different model family.
It outputs a probability; the threshold makes the decision.

mcq.q: What is σ(0), the sigmoid of zero?
options: e (about 2.72)
distractors: σ approaches 1 only for large positive inputs.
σ approaches 0 only for large negative inputs.
The sigmoid's output is always between 0 and 1.

mcq.q: What two steps does k-means alternate?
options: Compute the gradients, then update every centre's weights
Assign points to the nearest centre, then move each centre to their mean
Sort the points by distance, then count them in each region
Split the points on a feature, then prune the smallest groups
mcq.why: It stops when assignments stop changing.
distractors: That is gradient descent; k-means needs no gradients.
k-means does not sort points.
That is how decision trees are built.

mcq.q: How does gradient boosting differ from a random forest?
options: Boosting grows one very deep tree, while a forest uses many shallow ones
Boosting adds trees one by one to fix earlier errors; a forest averages independent trees
They are the same method under two names, both averaging many trees
A forest corrects errors one tree at a time; boosting averages its trees
mcq.why: Forests average many trees on random subsets; boosting stacks trees on residual errors.
distractors: Boosting adds many trees, usually shallow.
One is sequential, the other averages independent trees.
That swaps the two methods.

mcq.q: For tabular data, which is usually the strongest practical choice?
options: An LLM prompt with the table pasted in
Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM)
k-means clustering on the table
A single deep decision tree
mcq.why: Gradient boosting usually wins on structured tables.
distractors: LLMs are costly and weaker on tabular prediction.
k-means finds groups; it does not predict a label.
One deep tree overfits; boosted ensembles are stronger.

mcq.q: 88% of tickets are “general”. A classifier reports 91% accuracy. What is the real gain over the majority-class baseline?
options: 91 percentage points
9 percentage points
12 percentage points
3 percentage points
mcq.why: Always predicting “general” already scores 88%, so the model adds 3 points, and rare-class recall may still be poor.
distractors: That ignores the baseline.
That compares with 82%, which is not the baseline.
That is 100 − 88.

mcq.q: A sophisticated model barely beats a simple baseline. What should you conclude?
options: It adds little so far; check per-class results and costs
It is clearly better, since it beats the baseline
Accuracy is the only result that matters here
The baseline must be wrong if it scores so well
mcq.why: Report the baseline next to every result; if the gain is tiny, the complexity may not be worth it.
distractors: A tiny gain may not justify the cost and complexity.
Per-class results and costs can tell a different story.
Strong baselines are common; that is why you report them.

mcq.q: In the k-means figure, you choose a k that does not match the true groups. What happens?
options: k-means still returns tidy-looking clusters
It refuses to run
All points join one cluster
It finds the true number of groups automatically
mcq.why: k-means always produces k clusters, so clean-looking clusters do not prove real structure.
distractors: It runs for any k.
Points are spread across all k centres.
k must be chosen; it is not discovered.

mcq.q: A tuned model is measured on validation data, and the baseline on a different test set. What is wrong?
options: Unfair: both must be measured on the same data
Nothing, as long as both scores are reported
The baseline does not need to be measured at all
Validation data is always harder than test data
mcq.why: Different data gives different difficulty; compare like with like.
distractors: The scores come from different data, so they cannot be compared.
Without a baseline you cannot tell whether the model adds value.
Neither set is harder by design; the issue is that they differ.

interview.q: Compare regression, classification and clustering, with an example of each.

Boosting usually stronger on tabular data

covers: Shows whether the model adds value

Recall at a usable precision, not accuracy

mcq.q: What does error analysis involve?
options: Sampling failures, tagging causes, counting them and fixing the biggest
Increasing the model's size until the failures go away
Re-running training with new random seeds and keeping the best
Reading only the most confident correct predictions
mcq.why: The biggest bucket, weighted by impact, tells you what to fix next.
distractors: Size does not tell you what is failing or why.
A new seed changes noise, not the causes of errors.
Error analysis looks at failures.

mcq.q: Why compute metrics per slice?
options: Averages are always misleading for any model
Slices replace the need for a test set
Slices make the model run faster in production
An average can hide a group where the model fails badly
mcq.why: A model at 89% overall may be far worse on mixed-language or new-product inputs.
distractors: Averages are useful; they can just hide a failing group.
Slices are computed on the test set.
Slicing is an evaluation step; it does not change the model.

mcq.q: Hyperparameters should be tuned on…
options: The training set's own score after each run
Live production traffic, measured per setting
The test set, checked once for each setting
The validation set (or cross-validation)
mcq.why: Touch the test set once; tune on validation.
distractors: Training scores reward memorising.
Tuning on live traffic risks harm and leaks into evaluation.
The test set is for one final estimate.

mcq.q: Why is random search often better than grid search per trial?
options: It always finds the global optimum, given enough trials
It is deterministic, so every run gives the same result
It tries more distinct values of the parameters that matter
It needs no validation set to score each of the trials
mcq.why: When only a few hyperparameters matter, random sampling tries more of their values in the same budget.
distractors: No search method guarantees that.
Random search is random; that is not its advantage.
Every trial is still scored on validation data.

mcq.q: Covariate shift means…
options: The inputs change, such as a new region
The class balance changes
The link between inputs and labels changes
The model's own code changes
mcq.why: The input distribution moves, so the model sees regions it rarely trained on.
distractors: That is label (prior) shift.
That is concept drift.
That is a deployment change, not a data shift.

mcq.q: Fraud suddenly spikes from 0.5% to 2% of transactions with the same tactics. This is…
options: Concept drift
Covariate (input) shift
Label (prior) shift
Data leakage
mcq.why: The class balance changed; the input-label relationship did not.
distractors: The tactics, and so the input–label link, are unchanged.
The rise is in the share of fraud, not in the inputs.
Nothing from the future leaked into training.

mcq.q: Fraudsters adopt a new tactic that old features do not capture. This is…
options: Overfitting
Covariate shift only
Label shift only
Concept drift
mcq.why: The relationship between inputs and the label has changed.
distractors: Overfitting is about training, not the world changing.
Inputs may look normal while the meaning changes.
Balance alone did not change.

mcq.q: A document classifier drops from 92% to 84% after scanned PDFs rise from 5% to 30% of traffic. What does the topic recommend?
options: Ignore it, since averages fluctuate from week to week anyway
Fix OCR, add scanned samples to training and a scanned slice to the dashboard
Raise the learning rate and retrain on the same training data
Switch to a larger model and change nothing else in the pipeline
mcq.why: Error analysis showed most new errors were scanned documents, so fix data and monitor that slice.
distractors: An 8-point drop tied to a traffic shift is a real slice failure.
The data lacks scanned documents; retraining as before will not fix that.
The problem is OCR and missing training data, not capacity.

mcq.q: An input-drift alarm fires. What is the right first response?
options: Measure performance: drift is a reason to check, not proof of a drop
Disable the model until the cause of the drift is explained
Retrain immediately on the newest data you have
Ignore it, since some input drift is always normal
mcq.why: Inputs can drift without harming accuracy, and accuracy can fall without visible input drift.
distractors: Drift alone does not prove the model got worse.
Retraining blindly may not help, and needs labels.
It is a reason to check performance.

mcq.q: When is cross-validation most useful?
options: When data is small
Only for LLMs
When data is huge
Never for tuning
mcq.why: It reuses scarce data for more reliable estimates; with lots of data a single validation split is often enough.
distractors: It applies to many model types.
With lots of data it is often unnecessary.
It is a standard tuning tool.

covers: Fix the biggest, often in the data
Re-evaluate on the same test set and slices
